description: We are two Grade 12 students who built a health monitor for long space missions. Tyler Lee started coding at 5 and has built and competed with robots for 11 years, winning international and Worlds awards. He led design, architecture, UI and machine learning. Justin Yueh, aspiring to enter medicine, co-built the health dashboards, researching health indicators, NASA HRP hazards and alerts. Our idea: Rokid glasses as passive, first-person health logging, so crews act without waiting for Earth.
summary:
The Einsteiner is a health monitoring system for a Mars crew that cannot wait for advice from Earth. In transit to Mars, a message to the flight surgeon  can take up to 22 minutes each way, so the crew has to notice problems and act on them alone. The system has five parts. AR glasses log a crew member’s day, a watch gives three first steps when something goes wrong, a crew dashboard checks every reading against that person’s expected line for the mission day, an offline medical aid opens NASA’s own treatment cards, and a smartphone does the processing. 
Alert levels are fixed, and cited NASA limits are checked by code so the system works with no AI model or link to Earth. Everything runs inside a real-time 3D mission (Earth apartment, Starship, Mars colony) that serves as the simulator. A “What-if” digital twin shows how exercise, shielding, sleep, and mission length can change bone, muscle, fitness, radiation dose, and other metrics. Each of NASA’s 17 human-research roadmap risks is mapped to the parts of the system that address it, so a flight surgeon can view what is monitored and what is not.
details:
What Einsteiner Does

The Einsteiner monitors a crew of four through a Mars mission and tells each person, in plain words, whether a vital reading is On Track, Watch, or Needs action, as well as providing suggestions on what to do next.

Sees

The crew wears AR glasses. On-device vision models can:

  • recognize objects, posture, and the room the wearer is in
  • read QR-signed equipment and medical device screens
  • log meals, drinks, and medicine from a plate, barcode, or NASA package code
  • flag a crewmate who may be down
Measures

The app collects heart rate, SpO2, and stress and breathing rate from a Garmin watch. SpO2, stress, and breathing rate need the team's Connect IQ watch app. One crewmate's baseline uses a consenting wearer's real Garmin averages; every other vital sign is simulated. It also runs fitness-for-duty tests in the glasses: a reaction-time test (PVT), a sit-to-stand test, a tandem walk, eye charts in the glasses, and urine colour read by the camera. Each reading is compared with the crew member's own expected line and with NASA's limit lines. The reaction-time result is shown against the CSA PRET open dataset (50 ground participants).

Decides

Code checks every reading against cited limits, such as cabin CO2 of 3 mmHg as a 1-hour average, radiation dose limits, and the unstable-vital-sign criteria in HRP-48044. Some limits are adjusted for spaceflight: the fever line is raised by 1°C because core body temperature runs higher in space (Stahn 2017). On the watch, an alert shows only three first steps and whom to tell. No model is involved.

Treats

The offline medical aid takes a described problem or a one-tap emergency button and returns NASA's treatment card verbatim, with page references, medicine checks, and a flag to contact the crew medical officer or the surgeon. Its 64 cards come from the ISS Medical Checklist (15), the Space Shuttle Medical Checklist (41), and HRP-48044. The model only finds the right card. If an answer contains a dose that is not in NASA's text, the app removes it. Research prototype: no clinician has review the cards, and 35 of the 64 have not yet been re-checked against the source.

Plans

The What-If page is a digital twin of each crew member. Change the exercise days, bisphosphonate use, water-wall shielding, storm-shelter hours, sleep or transit time, and see how each risk responds. Each response is drawn from a published rate, or labelled as an assumption where none exists. For example, hip bone loss is 0.64% per month from NASA's bone fracture evidence report, and the drug's protection is bounded by the 5.5 months it was measured for (LeBlanc 2013). Risks are set pre crew member: after Shuttle flights, more than 80% of women but only about 20% of men were light-headed on standing (Waters 2002), so the landing risk is higher for female crew.

Oversees

One dashboard has four views:

  • Crew glasses: the camera feed and what the app works out from it.
  • Crew monitor: one status word and sentence, one action, six tiles (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood), a body map, and exercise, fluid, and vitamin D rings. Regular crew can only see their own data.
  • Medical officer: each crew member's vitals table, with the source of each limit (NASA requirement, clinical guideline, team rule, or model estimate). Also trends, model risk scores labelled "Model estimate", signed notes, an alert queue, a "flag to ground" summary with the current delay, and the medical-aid log.
  • Mission control: one board with the mission day, phase, and delay. It has crew cards with fitness for the next task, alerts ranked by mission impact with the medical officer's acknowledgement, a consult queue, cabin CO2 and radiation.

How it Works

Our system is designed to be worn. AR glasses are the crew members' main screen: alerts, measurement prompts, and device read-backs appear in their line of sight, so they never have to stop a task to check a tablet. Because judging is remote and judges may not have the glasses, we have prepared a demo of the heads-up display that shows what the wearer would see through the glasses.

  1. Edge: the crew hub runs Gemma 4 E4B through local Ollama. Gemma 4 12B stands in for the ship's server. Speech-to-text (Whisper) and the vision models run in the browser. Nothing on the safety path requires internet access. optional cloud models (Gemma 4 31B on the Gemini API, Claude for the photo scan) are used only for non-safety features when a key is set
  2. Answers come from NASA documents: free-text answers draw only on a retrieval index of NASA documents, and every answer carries citations.
  3. Real NASA data is replayed through the simulation:
    • A real day of ISS dose rate (TEPC)
    • Mars surface dose measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument
    • Real ISS cabin CO2 from NASA OSDR
  4. Simulated data is labeled: every simulated vital sign is marked SIM on screen

Benefits

  • Autonomy: the crew gets first steps in seconds, not after a round trip to Earth, which can take 44 minutes
  • Reliability: every limit and treatment card can be traced to a NASA document or a named clinical norm
  • Coverage: the risks page shows each of the 17 HRP risks under NASA's 5 hazards, with its coverage (6 fully, 10 partially, 1 none) and the files that address it
  • On Earth: the same kit covers heat stop-work rules for outdoor workers, a fatigue check before a drive, and home blood pressure and memory care

Intended Impact

We want a medical assistant that a small, isolated crew can trust because it is open about everything that it does:

  • It shows its sources
  • It labels simulated data
  • It keeps AI models away from safety decisions
  • It keeps working when the link to Earth is down

Tools, SDKs and Resources

Visual assets, 3D models and audio: Adobe Stock (images, Standard License), Sketchfab and GrabCAD (3D models), and ElevenLabs (AI-generated voice and audio). The SDKs, AI models and data services we used are listed with links under Other Data. Also used: zod, ZXing, jsQR and node-qrcode in the app; Google Fonts (SIL OFL 1.1); and PyTorch, timm, ONNX, Blender, glTF Transform, meshoptimizer and cadquery-ocp to train the models and build the 3D assets. All libraries are open source (MIT or Apache-2.0) except the Garmin FIT SDK (FIT Protocol License) and GSAP (Standard no-charge License), which are free to use but not OSI-approved.
